prompt: What is the shell?
body: The shell is a program that reads a line of text, runs a program, and prints the result. Commands have a shape: a program name, then optional flags that tweak behaviour, then arguments that name the targets. Flags usually start with a single dash and a letter (-r) or a double dash and a word (--recursive), and short flags can often be combined: `ls -l -a -h` is the same as `ls -lah`. When a command surprises you, do not guess: `command --help` prints a short summary and `man command` prints the full manual.

hints.text: Think about who is doing the reading when you type a command.

check.prompt: In `rm -r old-build`, what does the -r flag likely do?
check.answer: It makes the removal recursive, so it descends into directories.

prompt: You cannot remember cp's options. Which command prints a quick usage summary?

hints.text: The command comes first; the flag asking for help comes after it.
Almost every command accepts the double-dash word --help.

explanation: `cp --help` prints a usage summary. `man cp` gives the full manual.

prompt: A colleague runs `ls -lah`. What does that command do?

options.text: One flag named lah, which ls does not know
Three short flags combined: long output, all entries, human-readable sizes
It lists only files whose names contain a, h, or l

hints.text: Short flags after a single dash can be stacked into one cluster.

explanation: -l is long format, -a shows hidden entries, -h prints sizes in human units. Combined: `ls -lah`.

prompt: Which single letter is the usual short flag for running a command recursively?
modelAnswer: r, as in rm -r or cp -r

hints.text: Think of the word that means into every subdirectory.

explanation: -r (or --recursive) tells tools like rm, cp, and grep to descend into directories.

prompt: Absolute and relative paths
body: Every directory has a location, and `pwd` prints where you are. A path that starts with / is absolute: it is read from the root of the filesystem, so `/Users/ai/reports/2026.md` means the same thing no matter where you stand. A path without a leading slash is relative: it starts from your current directory, so `reports/2026.md` only works if reports is right here. Two short names save typing: ~ expands to your home directory, and .. means the parent of the current directory.

hints.text: Ask of any path: where does the walk start?

check.prompt: You are in /home/ai/lab and run `cd ../docs`. Where do you end up?

prompt: You are in /home/ai/lab. Where does `cd ..` take you?

hints.text: .. climbs exactly one level, not all the way to the top.

explanation: .. is the parent directory. From /home/ai/lab one step up is /home/ai.

prompt: Which of these is an absolute path?

hints.text: Look at the first character of each path.

explanation: A leading slash anchors the walk at the filesystem root, which makes it absolute.

prompt: What does `cd ~/projects` do?

options.text: Enters a folder literally named ~ in the current directory
Enters the projects folder inside your home directory

hints.text: The shell replaces ~ with something before cd even runs.

explanation: ~ expands to your home directory, so this is /home/<you>/projects on Linux or /Users/<you>/projects on macOS.

prompt: Move from one project to its sibling: you are in ~/dev/cairn and want ~/dev/notes.

steps.title: Confirm where you are
steps.body: Run `pwd`. It prints /home/<you>/dev/cairn so you know your anchor.

steps.title: Climb one level
steps.body: Run `cd ..`. You are now in ~/dev, the shared parent.

steps.title: Drop into the sibling
steps.body: Run `cd notes`. Relative paths start from where you stand.

steps.title: Or do it in one move
steps.body: `cd ../notes` combines the climb and the drop: go up, then sideways.

checkpoint.prompt: In one command, how do you go from ~/dev/cairn to ~/dev/notes?

hints.text: The parent directory is the meeting point between siblings.
Both paths end with a folder inside the same directory.

scaffolds.prompt: Which directory is the shared parent of ~/dev/cairn and ~/dev/notes?
Starting in ~/dev/cairn, which single command lands you in ~/dev/notes?

hints.text: You must climb out of cairn before you can enter notes.

prompt: In your own words: what makes a path absolute, what does ~ expand to, and what does .. mean?
modelAnswer: An absolute path starts at the filesystem root (/) and works from anywhere. ~ expands to the current user's home directory before the command runs. .. names the parent of the current directory.

hints.text: Three things to cover: the anchor, the home shortcut, and the parent shortcut.

hints.text: Work through the commands one at a time and watch pwd change.

prompt: Reading an ls listing
body: Plain `ls` shows visible names only. Files whose names start with a dot are hidden: configs like .gitignore or .env do not appear until you add -a. The -l flag switches to long format, one file per line: permissions, link count, owner, group, size, modification date, then the name. Add -h so sizes print as 4.0K instead of 4096. Two power moves: -S sorts by size (largest first) and -t sorts by modification time (newest first).

hints.text: The leading dot is the only thing that hides a file from plain ls.

check.prompt: Why does `ls` not show .env but `ls -a` does?
check.answer: Names starting with a dot are hidden from the plain listing; -a shows all entries.

prompt: Which command shows hidden files in a directory?

hints.text: One short flag means all.

explanation: `ls -a` lists all entries, including dot files like .gitignore.

prompt: A teammate says their project has no .env file, but the app insists it does. What is the fastest check?

options.text: ls, because .env would be listed by name
ls -a, because names starting with a dot are hidden from plain ls
ls .env/ since env files live in a folder

hints.text: The file name starts with a character plain ls treats specially.

explanation: Dot files are invisible to plain `ls`; `ls -a` settles the argument instantly.

prompt: You want sizes you can read at a glance. Which listing prints sizes like 4.0K and 12M?

options.text: ls -l, which always prints human sizes

hints.text: Long output prints raw bytes until you add the human flag.

explanation: -l gives the detail columns and -h renders sizes in K, M, and G.

prompt: Lab: inspect a directory fully

hints.text: Create the hidden file first, then compare plain ls with ls -a.

prompt: Reading files without opening an editor
body: `cat` dumps a whole file to the screen, which is perfect for short files and useless for 10,000-line logs. For those, take slices: `head -n 20 file` prints the first 20 lines and `tail -n 20 file` prints the last 20. `less file` opens a pager where you scroll with arrows, search with /pattern, and quit with q. When you need facts rather than content, `wc` counts: -l lines, -w words, -c bytes.

hints.text: head and tail are symmetric: one reads from the top, one from the bottom.

check.prompt: A build log has 40,000 lines and the error is at the end. Which command shows you the last 30 lines?

prompt: Which command prints the last 20 lines of server.log?

hints.text: The end of a fish is its tail.

explanation: tail reads from the bottom; -n 20 asks for twenty lines.

prompt: Which command counts the lines in notes.txt?

hints.text: The flag letter matches the unit you want.

explanation: -l counts lines, -w words, -c bytes.

prompt: You need to scroll through a 5,000-line config looking for one setting. Which tool fits best?

options.text: cat config.yaml, then read the terminal scrollback
less config.yaml, then search inside with /setting

hints.text: You want paging and search, not a one-shot dump.

explanation: less pages through the file and searches with /pattern. tail -f follows new output on a live log, which is a different job.

hints.text: Run the setup line first so the sample file exists.

prompt: grep: find lines that match
body: `grep pattern file` prints every line of the file containing the pattern. Order matters: pattern first, then the file. The flags you will use daily: -i ignores case, -n prints line numbers, -c counts matching lines, -v inverts the match (lines without the pattern), and -r searches every file under a directory. To find TODO notes across a whole project: `grep -rn TODO .`

hints.text: Say the command as a sentence: find, in this file, the lines containing this.

check.prompt: What does `grep -c error app.log` print: the matching lines, or a count?
check.answer: A count of matching lines, not the lines themselves

prompt: Which command searches for TODO in every file under the current directory?

hints.text: Directories need a flag that says: go inside them too.

explanation: -r makes grep walk the directory tree. The dot means start here.

prompt: Logs contain error, Error, and ERROR. Which command catches all three?

hints.text: One flag ignores case differences.

explanation: -i makes the match case-insensitive. -v would print the lines without error, the opposite of what you want.

prompt: Which grep line is written correctly?

hints.text: What are you looking for, and where? Match that order.

explanation: grep takes the pattern first, then the file.

prompt: Lab: hunt TODOs in a small tree

hints.text: Combine -r, -n, and -i in one flag cluster.

prompt: Pipes and redirection
body: Two characters turn small commands into tools. The pipe | feeds one command's output into the next command's input: `ls | wc -l` counts entries. Redirection sends output to a file instead: `ls > list.txt` writes (overwriting anything there) and `ls >> list.txt` appends to the end. A pipe connects commands; a redirect connects a command to a file. The classic counting pipeline is `sort | uniq -c`, because uniq only collapses lines that are adjacent, which is why you sort first.

hints.text: Ask what is on the right side: a command, or a file?

check.prompt: In `grep error app.log | wc -l`, what does wc receive?
check.answer: The matching lines from grep, as input, and it counts them

prompt: Which command saves the listing into list.txt, replacing any previous contents?

hints.text: The arrow points at a file, not at another command.

explanation: > redirects output to a file and overwrites it. A pipe needs a command on the right, and >> appends instead of replacing.

prompt: You log one line per run and must keep every earlier line. Which redirect keeps history?

hints.text: One arrow replaces; what might two arrows do?

explanation: >> appends. Every run with > would leave a one-line file.

prompt: What does `cat notes.txt | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -n 5` show?

options.text: The five largest files mentioned in notes.txt
The five most frequent lines in notes.txt, with counts
The first five lines of notes.txt unchanged

hints.text: Read the pipeline left to right; each stage transforms the previous stage's output.

explanation: sort groups identical lines, uniq -c counts each group, sort -nr puts the biggest count first, head keeps five.

prompt: Lab: build a word-frequency pipeline

hints.text: Build the pipeline one stage at a time and look at the output between stages.

prompt: Creating, copying, moving
body: Four verbs cover most file work. `mkdir -p a/b` creates nested directories in one shot. `touch draft.md` creates an empty file. `cp source dest` copies a file; add -r to copy a directory and everything inside it. `mv old new` moves or renames, and unlike cp it removes the original. Delete with `rm file`, and know that rm is permanent: there is no trash and no undo. Before any risky delete, run `ls` on the exact path you are about to type.

hints.text: cp duplicates; mv relocates. Only one of them leaves the original behind.

check.prompt: What is the difference between `cp a.txt b.txt` and `mv a.txt b.txt`?
check.answer: cp leaves both files; mv leaves only b.txt

prompt: You want a backup of report.md before editing it. Which command keeps the original?

hints.text: A backup is a copy by definition.

explanation: cp duplicates the file and leaves the original in place. mv would leave only the .bak file.

prompt: Which command renames draft-v1.md to draft-v2.md?

hints.text: Renaming is moving to a new name in the same directory.

explanation: mv with a new name in the same directory is a rename. cp would leave the old file behind.

prompt: Which command copies the whole photos directory, including everything inside?

hints.text: Into every subdirectory: which flag word from earlier means that?

explanation: Directories need recursive copy: cp -r. Plain cp refuses or copies only single files.

prompt: Lab: build and move a mini project

hints.text: Run the commands in order and verify each step with ls before moving on.

prompt: find: walk the tree
body: `find` searches by file properties rather than by content. It always needs a starting directory: `find . -name "*.log"` walks the current tree printing every .log file. Useful tests: -type f for files only, -type d for directories only, -iname for case-insensitive names, and -size +10M for anything over ten megabytes. Quote the pattern, as in "*.log", so the shell does not expand it before find sees it.

hints.text: find answers where is it, not what is inside it. Content search is grep's job.

check.prompt: Which find command lists only directories under the current tree?

prompt: Which command finds every .log file under the current directory?

hints.text: The first thing after find is where to start walking.

explanation: find needs the starting point: `find . -name "*.log"`. Without the dot it errors; with a bare glob the shell expands it first.

prompt: Which find command lists files only, skipping directories?

hints.text: f for files, d for directories.

explanation: -type f filters to regular files.

prompt: Lab: find and size log files

hints.text: Create the nested tree first, then predict what find will print before running it.

prompt: Permission bits and safe habits
body: `ls -l` starts each line with ten characters. The first is the type (- for files, d for directories); the rest are three triads of rwx: read, write, execute, for owner, group, and others. So -rw-r--r-- means the owner can read and write, everyone else can only read. Numbers are shorthand: r=4, w=2, x=1, added per triad, so 644 is rw- r-- r-- and 755 is rwx r-x r-x. `chmod +x script.sh` adds execute for everyone. `sudo` runs one command as root: powerful, and worth asking why before using it. `rm` has no trash; only backups bring files back.

hints.text: Read the ten characters in groups: type, owner, group, others.

check.prompt: What can a non-owner do with a file listed as -rw-r--r--?
check.answer: Read it, but not write or execute it

prompt: A file shows -rw-r--r-- in ls -l. Who can write to it?

options.text: Nobody, because there is no x

hints.text: Find the w in each of the three triads.

explanation: The first triad (owner) is rw-. Group and others have r-- only, so only the owner can write.

prompt: Running ./deploy.sh fails with permission denied. Which fix adds execute permission?

hints.text: The error names the missing permission: add exactly that.

explanation: chmod +x adds execute. 644 is the read/write default with no execute bit, and sudo does not fix permissions at all.

prompt: A command fails because a file belongs to root. What does sudo do?

options.text: Speeds the command up so it succeeds
Runs that one command with root's permissions
Permanently changes the file's owner to you

hints.text: sudo is about identity, not about effort.

explanation: sudo runs the single command that follows as the superuser. Use it deliberately, not as a retry habit.

prompt: You just ran `rm notes-old.txt` by mistake. Where can you restore it from?

options.text: Nowhere, unless you have a backup; rm is permanent
It is still on disk until you empty a bin directory

hints.text: The shell has no undo and no recycling step.

explanation: rm unlinks the file immediately. Backups, or nothing, are the recovery path.

prompt: Teach it back: decode -rw-r--r--, say what 755 means in bits, and describe when sudo is appropriate.
modelAnswer: -rw-r--r--: the owner reads and writes, the group and others only read. 755 is rwx for the owner, r-x for group and others, from r=4, w=2, x=1. sudo is for deliberate admin actions on files owned by root, used once and questioned first.

hints.text: Three parts: the triads, the number-to-bits conversion, and the sudo rule of thumb.
